Glossary

Website and hosting terms, explained simply

29 terms that come up when you set up a domain, hosting, email or website, each explained in plain English with a link to the guide that covers it.

ABCDFHMNP#STUW

A

A record
A DNS record that points a domain name to the IP address of the server hosting your website. Learn more

B

Backup
A saved copy of your website files and database that can be restored if something breaks. Good backups run automatically, are stored off the server and are tested by restoring them. Learn more

C

Caching
Storing ready-made copies of pages so they load faster for visitors instead of being rebuilt on every request. Learn more
CDN (content delivery network)
A network of servers around the world that stores copies of your site's files so pages load faster for visitors far from your host. Learn more
CMS (content management system)
Software for editing a website without writing code. WordPress is the most widely used CMS. Learn more
Core Web Vitals
Google's measurements of loading speed, responsiveness and visual stability, used as part of how it evaluates page experience. Learn more

D

DKIM
DomainKeys Identified Mail. A digital signature added to outgoing email that lets receiving servers confirm the message came from your domain and wasn't altered. Learn more
DMARC
A DNS record that tells receiving mail servers what to do with email that fails SPF or DKIM checks (monitor, quarantine or reject) and sends you reports. Learn more
DNS (Domain Name System)
The internet's address book. DNS records tell browsers where your website lives and tell mail servers where to deliver your email. Learn more
Domain registrar
The company you register and renew your domain name with. It is often separate from your web host. Learn more

F

Firewall (WAF)
A web application firewall filters malicious traffic before it reaches your site, blocking common attacks and abusive bots. Learn more

H

Honeypot
A hidden form field that people never see but spam bots fill in, letting the form reject automated submissions without a CAPTCHA. Learn more
HTTPS
The secure version of HTTP. It encrypts data sent between a visitor's browser and your website using an SSL/TLS certificate. Learn more

M

Malware
Malicious software injected into a website, often through outdated plugins or stolen passwords, to spam, redirect or steal data. Learn more
Managed WordPress hosting
Hosting where the provider handles server maintenance, caching, backups and security for WordPress sites. It usually costs more than shared hosting. Learn more
MX record
The DNS record that tells the internet which servers receive email for your domain. Learn more

N

Nameservers
The servers that hold your domain's DNS records. Changing nameservers moves control of your DNS to a different provider. Learn more

P

Plugin
An add-on that extends WordPress, such as a contact form, SEO tool or security scanner. Every plugin needs updates, so keep only what you use. Learn more

#

301 redirect
A permanent redirect from one web address to another. It sends visitors and search engines to the new URL and passes along most ranking signals. Essential when you change domains or page addresses. Learn more

S

Shared hosting
Low-cost hosting where many websites share the same server resources. Fine for small sites, with fewer performance and security guarantees. Learn more
SPF
Sender Policy Framework. A DNS record listing the servers allowed to send email for your domain, which helps stop spoofing. Learn more
SSL/TLS certificate
The certificate that enables HTTPS. Browsers warn visitors when it is missing or expired. Learn more
Staging site
A private copy of your website used to test updates and changes before they go live. Learn more

T

TLD (top-level domain)
The ending of a domain name, such as .com, .law or .attorney. Learn more
TTL (time to live)
How long DNS answers are cached. Lowering the TTL before a hosting move makes the switch take effect faster. Learn more
Two-factor authentication (2FA)
A second login step, such as a code from an app, that protects accounts even if a password is stolen. Learn more

U

Uptime monitoring
A service that checks your site regularly and alerts you when it goes down. Learn more

W

WCAG
The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, the widely used standard for making websites usable by people with disabilities.
WordPress.org vs WordPress.com
WordPress.org is the free, self-hosted software you install on your own hosting. WordPress.com is a hosted service run by Automattic with its own plans and limits. Learn more
